deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The previous page states a problem attributed to Franz Meyer. Iterated logarithms are defined by l(z)=log z for z>=1 and l(z)=1 for z<=1, with l_m the m-fold iterate. The task is to find a single function f(n) satisfying all of the infinitely many limit relations at once:
  lim n(f(n)-1) = 1,
  lim l(n)[n(f(n)-1)-1] = 1,
  lim ll(n){ l(n)[n(f(n)-1)-1] - 1 } = 1,
  and so on.
Read as a ratio test (f(n)=a_n/a_{n+1}), these are the successive Raabe, Bertrand, de Morgan and higher logarithmic tests. Meyer's claim is that one sequence can sit on the borderline of every test in the hierarchy simultaneously.

The previous page defines phi(n) as the largest even integer with l_{phi(n)}(n) > 2. It then notes that l_{phi/2}(l_{phi/2}(n)) > 2. Hence l_{phi(n)/2}(n) exceeds a tower e^e^...^e of height about phi(n)/2.

THIS PAGE, part 1.
(a) phi(n) grows with n, and so do l(phi(n)/2) and phi(n)/2. Precisely, these are non-decreasing and tend to infinity.
(b) A_n := floor(l_{phi(n)/2}(n)), the largest integer contained in l_{phi(n)/2}(n).
(c) Claim: the following f is the required function:
  f(n) = 1 + 1/n + 1/(n l_1 n) + 1/(n l_1 n l_2 n) + ... + 1/(n l_1 n ... l_N n).
  The upper index N of the last factor is written ambiguously, with both phi(n) and A_n near it.

Verification (my steps). Write P_{k,j} = l_{k+1}(n)...l_j(n), with P_{k,k} = 1. Define the k-th expression recursively:
  E_0 = n(f-1),
  E_k = l_k(n)(E_{k-1} - 1).
By telescoping, E_k = sum_{j=k}^{N} 1/P_{k,j} = 1 + sum_{j=k+1}^{N} 1/P_{k,j}.
So the k-th limit holds if and only if the tail T_k(n) = sum_{j=k+1}^{N} 1/(l_{k+1}n...l_j n) tends to 0 for every fixed k, while N = N(n) tends to infinity.

Take N = phi(n)/2 (my choice of reading). Then all factors l_j(n) with j <= N are >= l_N(n), which is >= a tower of height about N. Therefore T_k <= (N-k)/l_{k+1}(n) <= N/l_{k+1}(n), which tends to 0, since l_{k+1}(n) tends to infinity. In fact a uniform bound N/l_N(n) -> 0 also follows from the tower estimate.

The role of phi is a diagonal device. It makes the number of terms grow, but so slowly that every factor used stays large. This is a du Bois-Reymond-type diagonal construction.

THIS PAGE, part 2 (separate note). Let u=u(x,y), v=v(x,y) be a one-to-one ('umkehrbar eindeutig') analytic transformation of the whole x,y-domain onto the u,v-domain.
(a) Then u'=u, v'=v+f(u) is again such a transformation, for f any single-valued function defined for all u, e.g. an entire function. Its inverse is v=v'-f(u'). Reading the '+' is my interpretation of the hand; a multiplicative v*f(u) would require f never to vanish.
(b) Hilbert remarks that by successive application of such operations, together with the inversion u -> 1/u, v -> v, one easily produces maps such as (u,v) -> (u, v/u), (v, v/u), (v, 1/u). These are Cremona-type (birational) maps.
(c) He then asks, without a question mark, whether from the identity x=x, y=y one can derive ALL such transformations by finitely many such operations. This is a generation problem.
(d) Conclusion: 'there are therefore transcendental one-to-one transformations'. For example, (u, v+e^u) is a non-algebraic analytic automorphism of the plane (C^2). This contrasts with one variable, where automorphisms of C are affine.
errors:
Ambiguous upper index of the last term in f(n). The natural and correct choice is N = phi(n)/2 (or any N -> infinity with N/l_N(n) -> 0).

If N = A_n (about l_{phi/2}(n), which is far larger than phi(n)) were meant, the sum would run past index phi(n). With Hilbert's convention l(z)=1 for z<=1 but l(z)=log z in (0,1) for 1<z<e, some factor l_j(n) can then be arbitrarily small. The tail estimate is then unjustified.

The convention l(z)=1 for z<=1 is itself awkward, since l is discontinuous and dips below 1 on (1,e). It is harmless only if the indices stay <= phi(n)/2.
'phi(n) waechst mit wachsendem n' should read 'non-decreasing and unbounded'. phi is a step function, not strictly increasing; this does not affect the argument.

Part 2: maps like (u, v/u) or (v, 1/u) are not everywhere-defined bijections of the finite plane (they are singular at u=0). They are one-to-one only in a projective/birational sense, so the setting silently shifts between automorphisms of C^2 and Cremona transformations.

The generation question is posed but not answered. For all analytic automorphisms of C^2 the answer to 'finitely many such operations give all' is negative in general. Shears and linear maps generate only a proper (though dense) subgroup (Andersen-Lempert 1992). Only for polynomial automorphisms is the answer yes (Jung 1942; van der Kulk 1953).

results.what: Construction of a single f(n) satisfying simultaneously all logarithmic-scale limit relations n(f-1)->1, l n (n(f-1)-1)->1, ... i.e. a ratio a_n/a_{n+1} for which every test of the Raabe-Bertrand-de Morgan hierarchy is inconclusive; diagonal choice of the number of terms via phi(n).
results.modern_name: Incompleteness of the logarithmic scale of convergence tests; du Bois-Reymond diagonal construction (sequence beyond every member of a countable scale)
results.usually_credited_to: P. du Bois-Reymond (1873-1875, Infinitaercalcuel/scale theorems); A. Pringsheim (1890) for convergence tests; problem here attributed to Franz Meyer

results.what: Shear maps (u,v) -> (u, v+f(u)) with f entire are biholomorphic automorphisms of the plane; hence transcendental one-to-one analytic transformations of C^2 exist.
results.modern_name: Shears / elementary automorphisms; transcendental automorphisms of C^2 (Aut(C^2) much larger than Aut(C))
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore of 19th-century analysis; systematic theory Rosay-Rudin (1988), Andersen-Lempert (1992)

results.what: Question whether all one-to-one analytic (or birational) transformations of the plane are generated by finitely many elementary operations (shears, inversion u->1/u, swaps) starting from the identity.
results.modern_name: Generation problem for Aut(C^2) / Cremona group; tame vs wild automorphisms
results.usually_credited_to: Noether (1870) and Castelnuovo (1901) for the Cremona group; Jung (1942) and van der Kulk (1953) for polynomial automorphisms; Andersen-Lempert (1992) for density in the holomorphic case

deep.surprise_reason: The series construction is a standard du Bois-Reymond/Pringsheim-type diagonal argument, recorded as a solution of a problem posed by Meyer. The second note shows Hilbert, around the 1890s, explicitly using shears to get transcendental automorphisms of the plane. He also poses the finite-generation question that later became the Jung-van der Kulk and Andersen-Lempert circle. It is a notable early formulation, but it is only a question with an easy observation, not a result.

'ln', 'lln' in the formula denote iterated logarithms l_1 n, l_2 n, not natural log notation.
The last term's denominator index is written ambiguously (phi(n) above, A_n below). The likely intended reading is l_{phi(n)/2}(n), or the index A_n.
'so ist u [...] u [-v u-] v : v f(u)' most plausibly reads 'so ist u : u, v : v + f(u) ... wiederum eine solche Transformation' (shear map).
Insertion above the line: 'die Transformation v = v, u = 1/u'.
The sentence 'Kann man durch eine endliche Anzahl solcher Operationen aus der identischen Transformation x = x, y = y, sämmtliche ableiten' is a question; there is no question mark in the original.
